prompt.context: Your client is a major window manufacturer with significant market share. However, they are looking to grow revenues and have asked for your help.
prompt.question: How should the client grow its revenues?

clarifying_info.q: What types of windows does the company make?
clarifying_info.a: Three product lines: premium, mid-range, and economy — all for residential buildings. There is not significant differentiation in actual quality, but premium products have additional features.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client position its products?
clarifying_info.a: All lines are positioned based on superior functionality.
Through specialty retailers, hardware stores, and supercenters such as Home Depot.

clarifying_info.q: What does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: There are 3 large players and a large number of small mom-and-pop manufacturers.

clarifying_info.q: Does market share vary by region?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, significantly. See the regional share exhibit.

clarifying_info.q: Are all product segments the same size?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the overall size of each of the three segments is the same.

clarifying_info.q: Does the company operate outside the US?
clarifying_info.a: No, currently the company only distributes its product in the US.
Yes, the company is profitable and has been for many years.

exhibits.title: Regional Market Share by Product Line
exhibits.shows: A table showing the client's market share (%) across three US regions (South, Northeast, Midwest) and three product lines (Premium, Midrange, Economy).

framework: Understand the industry: market size, growth, competitive landscape, segments
Understand the company: product lines, positioning, distribution, profitability
Identify revenue growth levers: new geographies, new segments/products, increased share in weak segments, pricing
Assess each lever for feasibility, investment required, and fit with company strengths

questions.prompt: Why does the client have low market share in the South and in the economy segment?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates note the regional share pattern — high share in Northeast and Midwest, very low in the South — and probe for a root cause. The key insights are: (1) many of the windows are designed with features useful in cold regions, not hot ones, making them less attractive in the South; (2) the economy line windows are still more expensive than competitors, which offer very few features, so the client cannot compete on price in the economy tier.

questions.prompt: What are the main options for growing revenues?
questions.guidance: Candidates should generate a MECE set of growth levers. Strong answers include: (1) geographic expansion — specifically international markets (e.g., Canada) where cold-weather features are valued; (2) improving penetration in the South by redesigning/repositioning products for warm climates; (3) increasing share in the economy segment by reducing features and lowering cost/price; (4) organic growth in existing strong regions (Northeast, Midwest) where share is already high but still below 100%.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific actions could the client take to grow revenues?

categories.name: Acquisition
ideas: Acquire a small mom-and-pop player with strength in the South and economy segments
Target acquisition candidates with warm-climate product designs
Use existing profitability and scale to finance acquisition

categories.name: Product repositioning
ideas: Reduce features on economy line to lower cost and price below competitors
Redesign or create a warm-climate product line suited for the South
Reposition premium line to further differentiate from mid-range

categories.name: Geographic expansion
ideas: Expand internationally, starting with Canada where cold-weather features are valued
Target other cold-climate markets (Northern Europe, etc.) in a later phase
Grow presence in Midwest and Northeast where share is already strong

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Deepen relationships with supercenters (Home Depot) to increase shelf presence in the South
Explore direct-to-contractor channels in underpenetrated regions
Partner with regional specialty retailers in the South

recommendation: The client should pursue a three-pronged revenue growth strategy: (1) acquire a small competitor with strength in the South and economy segments, (2) strip features from the economy line to compete on price, and (3) expand internationally starting with Canada, where cold-weather window features are a competitive advantage.
risks: Acquisition integration risk — small mom-and-pop manufacturers may lack scalable operations or strong brand
Reducing features on economy line may erode brand perception across all lines
International expansion requires navigating different building codes, distribution networks, and customer preferences
Redesigning products for warm climates requires R&D investment and time to market
next_steps: Screen acquisition targets in the South with viable economy/warm-climate product portfolios
Conduct cost analysis to determine feature reduction potential on economy line
Run a pilot in one Southern market with a repositioned economy product
Evaluate Canadian market entry: regulatory requirements, distributor partnerships, demand sizing
